name: Bonnor's Magnetic Dipole
description: The static field of a mass with a magnetic dipole moment, the solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations William Bonnor found in 1966. Roberto Emparan showed in 2000 that its two poles are extremal black holes with opposite magnetic charges, held apart by a strut on the axis between them.
convention: The parameter $m$ is a length, and the mass $M$ has $GM/c^2 = 2m$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What does gravity make of a bar magnet, a body with a mass, a north pole, and a south pole? An exact answer came from William Bonnor in 1966, a static solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations with an axis of symmetry, set out in two pages [bonnor1966]. Seen from far away it is a body of mass $2m$ with a magnetic dipole moment $2mb$, in units with $G = c = 1$, and with $m = 0$ it is flat space [emparan2000]. Bonnor made it with a rule that turns a stationary vacuum solution into a static one with a magnetic field, the twist of the spinning source traded for the magnetic potential [bonnor2002]. Kerr's black hole is what goes into the rule, and the dipole keeps Kerr's two functions with the sign of $a^2$ reversed, $r^2 - 2mr - b^2$ and $r^2 - b^2\cos^2\theta$ [davidson1994, emparanteo2001].¶With $b = 0$ the dipole moment vanishes, and the mass that remains has higher multipoles and a naked singularity, so Schwarzschild's black hole is no member of the family [emparan2000]. The quadrupole moment of the mass is $2m(b^2 - m^2)$, fixed by the mass and the dipole moment, and it changes sign at $b = m$ [kovar2013]. In J. P. Ward's analysis of 1975 the source is a pair of magnetic poles of opposite sign that share the mass equally and stand a coordinate distance $2b$ apart [ward1975, kovar2013]. Bonnor saw that his metric is singular on the surface $r = r_+ = m + \sqrt{m^2 + b^2}$, where $r^2 - 2mr - b^2$ vanishes [emparan2000]. Where does that surface lie?¶Roberto Emparan's answer of 2000 is that the surface is a stretch of the axis itself: the rotations about the axis leave every point of $r = r_+$ where it is, and $\theta$ runs along the stretch from one pole to the other [emparan2000]. A small circle around that stretch is too long for its radius, by the factor $(1 + m^2/b^2)^2$ [emparan2000]. The extra angle is a strut, a rod under pressure that keeps the two poles from falling together [emparan2000]. The period of $\phi$ can be chosen to make the stretch smooth, and then angle is missing around the axis beyond each pole, as around a cosmic string that pulls the pole outward with tension $\tfrac{1}{4}\left(1 - b^4/(m^2 + b^2)^2\right)$ [emparan2000]. For $b$ much larger than $m$ the tension is $m^2/2b^2$, the inverse square law for two poles a distance of order $b$ apart [emparan2000].¶Close to either end of the stretch the geometry is the throat of an extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole, with a horizon drawn out along the axis into a prolate spheroid [emparan2000]. Each pole is therefore a black hole, the two carry the magnetic charges $\pm mr_+/b$, and Emparan named the pair a dihole [emparan2000, emparanteo2001]. The stretch between the holes is infinitely long because each throat is [emparan2000]. The horizons, he wrote, had "gone unnoticed in all previous literature" [emparan2000]. The same spacetime had turned up in 1989 in other coordinates, in the hands of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and Basilis Xanthopoulos, as two black holes of equal mass and opposite charge with a string along the axis that "provides support for the black holes", and neither of them recognised Bonnor's dipole in it [chandrasekhar1989, emparanteo2001].¶Can the strut be taken away? Two holes with charges of the same sign can stand in balance, their gravity pulling and their charges pushing, as in the solutions of Majumdar and Papapetrou, and between opposite charges both forces pull [emparan2000]. The push has to come from outside, and Emparan supplied it with a Harrison transformation, which sets the dihole in a magnetic field along its axis that far away is Melvin's magnetic universe [emparan2000]. Frederick Ernst had removed the conical singularity of the C-metric the same way in 1976 [ernst1976, emparan2000]. With the field set to $B = 2m/(r_+ + b)^2$ the whole axis is smooth, each horizon is a round sphere, and each throat is exactly Bertotti and Robinson's [emparan2000]. Emparan expected the balance to be unstable, with the dihole sitting on top of the barrier under which a magnetic field creates pairs of black holes [emparan2000].¶In 2001 Emparan and Edward Teo drew a pair of black holes of equal mass and opposite charge, with horizons that are not degenerate, out of the general solution of Vladimir Manko, Jesús Martín, and Eduardo Ruiz, and checked that Bonnor's dipole is the limit in which the horizons become degenerate [emparanteo2001, manko1994]. A dilaton joined the dipole in 1994 in the solution of Aharon Davidson and Edward Gedalin, which in Kaluza-Klein theory is the monopole and antimonopole pair of David Gross and Malcolm Perry [davidson1994, grossperry1983, emparan2000]. Test particles sent through the dipole by Jiří Kovář, Ondřej Kopáček, Vladimír Karas, and Yasufumi Kojima in 2013 can circle on stable orbits that hover off the equatorial plane, some of them geodesics [kovar2013]. Their motion is not integrable, and it turns chaotic as the energy of the particle is raised [kovar2013].

related.text: The dipole with $b = 0$, which is Zipoy and Voorhees's deformed mass at $q = 1$: a mass with a quadrupole and no magnet [emparan2000].

The spinning black hole Bonnor's rule starts from. The rule trades Kerr's twist for a magnetic potential, and the dipole keeps Kerr's two functions with $a^2$ turned into $-b^2$ [bonnor2002, davidson1994].
Each pole on its own. In the limit $b \to \infty$ the poles are infinitely far apart, and the neighbourhood of each is an extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole [emparan2000].
Extremal black holes with charges of one sign, which balance with no strut. Give two of them opposite charges and both forces pull, which is Bonnor's dipole [emparan2000].
The magnetic universe, which Bonnor found in 1954. Set in its field by a Harrison transformation, the dipole loses its strut at one field strength [bonnor1954, emparan2000].
The throat of an extremal charged black hole. Each pole of the dipole opens into such a throat, and with the pair balanced by an outside field it is exactly Bertotti and Robinson's [emparan2000].
Two black holes that accelerate apart. The dipole is the same pair at rest, and Emparan placed it on top of the barrier under which a magnetic field creates the accelerating pair [emparan2000].
A mass with no multipole beyond the monopole. The dipole with $b = 0$ keeps a quadrupole and a naked singularity, so it is not Schwarzschild's black hole [emparan2000].
The Weyl field of a point mass. In Weyl's coordinates each black hole of the dipole is a single point of the axis as well [emparanteo2001].
Gross and Perry's monopole of Kaluza-Klein theory. Their monopole and antimonopole pair is the dipole's counterpart in that theory [grossperry1983, emparan2000].

coordinates.name: Bonnor
domains: Z = 0 \;\text{(the axis between the black holes, with the strut)}

parameters.description: Half the mass as a length: the mass $M$ at spatial infinity has $GM/c^2 = 2m$
Dipole length, $b > 0$: the magnetic dipole moment is $2mb$ in units with $G = c = 1$, and the two black holes carry the magnetic charges $\pm m\left(m + \sqrt{m^2 + b^2}\right)/b$
Bonnor's first polynomial, an area, equal to $Z + b^2\sin^2\theta$; the magnetic potential is $A_\phi = 2mbr\sin^2\theta/P$ in units with $G = c = 1$
Bonnor's second polynomial, an area, equal to $Z + \left(m^2 + b^2\right)\sin^2\theta$
Bonnor's third polynomial, an area, equal to $P + 2mr$
Bonnor's fourth polynomial, an area, which vanishes at $r = m + \sqrt{m^2 + b^2}$, the axis between the two black holes

coordinates.convention: We use Bonnor's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length, in which Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = \sqrt{Z}\sin\theta$ and $z = (r - m)\cos\theta$, and write $P$, $Q$, $Y$, and $Z$ for his four polynomials in $r$ and $\cos\theta$. The length $b$ is the ratio of the magnetic dipole moment to the mass. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
